questions.question: According to Article 246 of the Indian Constitution, parliament has exclusive powers to make laws on subjects mentioned in which of the following lists?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Union List**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 246** of the Indian Constitution specifies the legislative powers of the Union and State governments.
 
• The **Union List** includes subjects on which only the **Parliament** has the exclusive power to legislate.
 
• Examples of subjects in the **Union List** include **defense, foreign affairs, atomic energy, railways, banking, and communication.**
 
• This exclusive power ensures a unified approach to critical subjects that impact the entire country.
 
• The **Union List** presently consists of **97 subjects** (as per the original Constitution, though amendments may have altered the number).
 
• It is crucial for maintaining the **sovereignty and integrity** of India by centralizing decision-making on essential matters.
 
• The subjects in the Union List are designed to address areas of national importance and ensure uniformity in governance across states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **State List**__

 __
 
• The **State List** includes subjects on which **State Legislatures** have exclusive power to legislate.
 
• Examples include **police, public health, agriculture, and local governments.**
 
• This list allows states to govern matters that are primarily regional in nature.
 
 
 
• **Local List**__
 __
 
• The term **Local List** is not officially recognized within the Indian Constitution.
 
• Local governance is primarily addressed through the **Panchayati Raj system** under the **73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments.**
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List**__
 
 
• The **Concurrent List** includes subjects on which both the **Parliament and State Legislatures** can legislate.
 
• Examples include **education, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, and adoption.**
 
• In case of a conflict, the law made by the **Parliament** prevails over the State law.

questions.question: Where is the headquarter of the National Human Rights Commission in India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**New Delhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)** of India was established on **12th October 1993** under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
 
• The NHRC's headquarters is located in **New Delhi**, the capital city of India.
 
• The commission aims to protect and promote **human rights**, which are guaranteed by the Constitution of India and embodied in international covenants.
 
• The NHRC operates autonomously and is tasked with investigating cases related to the violation of human rights across the country.
 
• Its headquarters is strategically located in New Delhi to ensure easy access to central government authorities and institutions for coordination and policy implementation.
 
• The NHRC headquarters is equipped with modern facilities to carry out its functions, including conducting inquiries, hearings, and maintaining records of cases.
 
• The NHRC has the power to make recommendations to the government regarding policies and measures for the protection of human rights.
 
• New Delhi serves as the administrative hub of India, making it an ideal location for the NHRC to function effectively.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mumbai**__

 __
 
• **Mumbai** is known as the financial capital of India and is home to the headquarters of many major banks and corporations.
 
• It houses important institutions like the Reserve Bank of India and the Bombay Stock Exchange.
 
• Although Mumbai is not the headquarters of NHRC, it plays a vital role in India's economic landscape.
 
 
 
• **Chennai**__
 __
 
• **Chennai**, located in Tamil Nadu, is known for its cultural heritage and is an important industrial and educational hub in southern India.
 
• The city is home to several national institutions such as IIT Madras and Anna University.
 
• While Chennai is significant for its contributions to education and industry, it is not the location of NHRC headquarters.
 
 
 
• **Kolkata**__
 
 
• **Kolkata**, the capital city of West Bengal, is known for its rich history and cultural significance.
 
• It was previously the capital of British India until 1911 and houses institutions like the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial.
 
• Despite its historical importance, Kolkata is not the location of the NHRC headquarters.

questions.question: Which of the following Directive Principles is mentioned in Article 43B of the Constitution of India?

options.text: Uniform civil code for the citizens
Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
Equal justice and free legal aid

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Promotion of co-operative societies**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 43B of the Constitution of India focuses on the **promotion of cooperative societies** as a Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• This provision emphasizes that the state shall endeavor to promote the formation and functioning of cooperative societies, ensuring their autonomy.
 
• Cooperative societies are recognized as instruments for socio-economic development, particularly in rural and agricultural sectors.
 
• The intent is to empower individuals and communities through collective efforts in areas such as agriculture, marketing, credit, and housing.
 
• This principle aligns with the broader goal of economic democracy and self-reliance enshrined in the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):** DPSPs are guidelines for the government to frame policies and laws aimed at achieving social and economic justice.
 
• **Cooperative Societies:** These are autonomous associations of persons united voluntarily to meet common economic, social, and cultural needs through jointly owned enterprises.
 
• **Role in Rural Development:** Cooperative societies play a key role in rural credit, agricultural marketing, and ensuring fair prices for farmers.
 
• **Constitutional Amendment:** The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act (2011) explicitly included the promotion of cooperative societies under Article 43B.
 
• **Autonomy and Accountability:** The amendment also aimed to provide legal and institutional safeguards to ensure the autonomy and accountability of cooperative societies.

questions.question: How does the President of India exercise his/her executive functions with respect to decision-making?

options.text: The President considers the advice of the Prime Minister and the Union council of ministers.
The President can repeatedly ask for reconsideration of any ministerial decision until satisfied.
The President acts entirely on his own absolute discretion
The President acts independently of the Union Government for foreign affairs.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The President considers the advice of the Prime Minister and the Union council of ministers.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The President of India exercises executive powers based on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers as per Article 74 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• While the President has the right to seek information and clarification, he/she cannot act independently of the advice provided by the Council of Ministers.
 
• The President may request the Council of Ministers to reconsider their advice but is bound to act according to the reconsidered advice.
 
• This ensures that the President’s role is largely ceremonial and decisions are aligned with parliamentary democracy principles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 74:** Specifies that the President must act according to the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
 
• **Ceremonial Role:** The President’s role is primarily ceremonial, representing the unity and integrity of the nation.
 
• **Reconsideration Power:** The President can return a decision for reconsideration once, but the advice is binding if resubmitted.
 
• **Checks and Balances:** The system ensures that the executive authority remains with the elected representatives while maintaining constitutional decorum.
 
• **Parliamentary Democracy:** India follows a parliamentary system where executive decisions are made by the elected government, not the President.

questions.question: What is the maximum imprisonment term that a Chief Judicial Magistrate can award?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**7 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) in India is empowered to pass sentences of imprisonment for a term of **up to 7 years**, as per Section 29(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973.
 
• The CJM also has the authority to impose fines and other penalties as prescribed by law, but the maximum term of imprisonment remains capped at 7 years.
 
• This jurisdiction of sentencing ensures that cases involving higher degrees of punishment are referred to Sessions Courts.
 
• The CJM typically handles cases classified as warrant cases, which involve offenses punishable with imprisonment exceeding 2 years but not exceeding 7 years.
 
• This limitation in sentencing authority is part of the tiered structure of the Indian judicial system, designed to distribute case handling based on the severity of offenses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hierarchy of Magistrates:**

 
 
• In India, Magistrates are categorized as Chief Judicial Magistrates (CJM), Judicial Magistrates of First Class, Judicial Magistrates of Second Class, and Executive Magistrates.
 
• The CJM is the highest-ranking judicial magistrate at the district level.
 
 
 
• **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC):**
 
 
• The CrPC, 1973, governs the procedural aspects of criminal law in India, including the powers and functions of various courts and magistrates.
 
 
 
• **Sessions Court:**
 
 
• Cases requiring imprisonment exceeding 7 years, life imprisonment, or death penalty are tried at Sessions Courts, which have higher sentencing authority than CJMs.
 
 
 
• **Warrant and Summons Cases:**
 
 
• Warrant cases involve offenses punishable by imprisonment exceeding 2 years, while summons cases are for less severe offenses.
 
• CJMs primarily handle warrant cases within their sentencing jurisdiction.

questions.question: Who among the following has the authority to specify an urban area as a 'large urban area' or a 'small urban area' or a 'transitional area' in a state?

options.text: Chief Justice of the State's High Court

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Governor of the State**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The authority to specify an urban area as a 'large urban area', 'small urban area', or 'transitional area' in a state is vested with the **Governor of the State**.
 
• This classification is made under the provisions of the **Constitution of India**, specifically Article 243Q.
 
• The Governor acts based on the recommendations of the state government and relevant demographic and administrative factors.
 
• Such classifications are essential for determining governance structures and resource allocation in urban local bodies.
 
• The Governor's decision takes into account criteria such as population density, revenue generation, and infrastructure needs of the area.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 243Q:**

 
 
• This article deals with the constitution of municipalities in urban areas.
 
• It mandates the classification of areas into transitional, small, and large urban areas for governance.
 
 
 
• **Urban Local Bodies:**
 
 
• These include municipal corporations, municipalities, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• The classification helps in determining the appropriate governance model for each type.
 
 
 
• **Governor's Role:**
 
 
• The Governor is the constitutional head of the state and acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
 
• In matters of urban area classifications, the Governor consults with state authorities for proper implementation.
 
 
 
• **Demographic Considerations:**
 
 
• Population density, infrastructure, and revenue generation are key factors in urban area classification.
 
• Such classifications impact the development plans and funding allocations for urban areas.
 
 
 
• **Urban Governance:**
 
 
• Effective urban governance ensures better resource management and development planning.
 
• It also helps in addressing challenges such as urban poverty, sanitation, and housing.

questions.question: Which Indian Constitutional Amendment Act have decreased the Fundamental Rights from seven to six?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**44th Constitutional Amendment Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1978 reduced the number of Fundamental Rights from seven to six.
 
• The amendment abolished the Fundamental Right to Property under Article 31 and moved it to the category of legal rights under Article 300A.
 
• The Fundamental Rights now include: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• This amendment was enacted during the Janata Party government to reverse some provisions introduced during the Emergency period (1975-1977).
 
• The 44th Amendment was aimed at strengthening the democratic framework and protecting individual rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and are essential for the development of individuals and the protection of their liberties.
 
• They are justiciable, meaning individuals can approach the courts for their enforcement.
 
• Originally, there were seven Fundamental Rights, but the Right to Property was removed as a Fundamental Right by the 44th Amendment.
 
 
 
• **44th Constitutional Amendment Act:**
 
 
• Enacted in 1978, it was introduced to undo the excesses of the 42nd Amendment passed during the Emergency.
 
• It aimed to restore the balance between the executive, legislature, and judiciary.
 
• It ensured that the proclamation of Emergency required stricter conditions and safeguarded citizens' rights during such times.
 
 
 
• **Right to Property:**
 
 
• Initially a Fundamental Right under Article 31, it guaranteed protection against arbitrary state actions regarding property.
 
• The 44th Amendment moved it to Article 300A, making it a legal right, thereby allowing the state to impose reasonable restrictions.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Amendment:**
 
 
• It marked a shift from authoritarian governance toward strengthening democratic principles.
 
• It provided safeguards to prevent misuse of constitutional provisions in the future.

questions.question: Which of the following systems was abolished by the Nineteenth Amendment Act, 1966?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Election tribunals.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Nineteenth Amendment Act, 1966** – This constitutional amendment abolished the Election Tribunals in India.
 
• Before this amendment, disputes related to the election of Members of Parliament and State Legislatures were decided by Election Tribunals.
 
• After the abolition, the jurisdiction to decide such disputes was transferred to the High Courts under the **Representation of the People Act, 1951.**
 
• The change was intended to streamline the process and ensure faster, more authoritative resolution of election disputes.
 
• This amendment came into effect on **11 December 1966.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Privy Purse System (Option 1):** Abolished by the 26th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971. Privy purses were payments made to former rulers of princely states as part of their agreement of accession to India.
 
• **Zamindari System (Option 2):** Abolished soon after independence through various Zamindari Abolition Acts passed by states during the early 1950s, aimed at land reforms and ending intermediary landlordism.
 
• **Separate Electorate System (Option 3):** Abolished by the Constitution of India in 1950; it was earlier introduced during British rule (e.g., Government of India Act, 1909) to give separate representation to communities, notably Muslims.
 
• **Election Tribunals: **Were quasi-judicial bodies created under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, to decide election disputes before the Nineteenth Amendment.
 
• **Amendment Procedure:** Constitutional amendments in India are passed under Article 368 of the Constitution.
 
• **Representation of the People Act, 1951:** Governs the conduct of elections in India, qualifications/disqualifications, and the process for resolving disputes.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the Official Language Commission in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 344**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 344** of the Indian Constitution deals with the formation of the Official Language Commission.
 
• The Commission is tasked with making recommendations to the President regarding the progressive use of Hindi and restrictions on the use of English in official purposes.
 
• The first Official Language Commission was constituted in **1955** under the chairmanship of B.G. Kher.
 
• Article 344 also mandates the President to appoint a Committee composed of members of Parliament to examine the recommendations of the Commission.
 
• This article plays a pivotal role in implementing the constitutional vision for promoting Hindi as the official language of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 343** of the Indian Constitution specifies Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of India.
 
• **Article 341** deals with the inclusion of Scheduled Castes in the Constitution, not language-related matters.
 
• **Article 342** pertains to the specification of Scheduled Tribes, unrelated to language provisions.
 
• The Official Language Act of **1963** further elaborates on the use of Hindi and English in official communications, ensuring linguistic inclusivity.
 
• The idea behind these constitutional provisions is to promote national integration while respecting linguistic diversity across India.

questions.question: Who among the following is the political head of the municipality in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chairman**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Chairman is the **political head of a municipality** in India, responsible for representing the elected members and presiding over meetings.
 
• The Chairman is chosen from among the elected members of the **Municipal Council**, which governs smaller towns or urban areas.
 
• They are tasked with ensuring that the municipality's policies and programs are implemented effectively and align with the needs of the local community.
 
• The Chairman works in collaboration with the Chief Municipal Officer (administrative head) to oversee the functioning of the municipality.
 
• This position is distinct from the Mayor, who is the political head of a Municipal Corporation in larger urban areas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Municipal Council:**

 
 
• A Municipal Council administers smaller urban areas, usually towns or cities with a population of 20,000 to 300,000.
 
• The council is composed of elected representatives, including the Chairman, who leads the council.
 
• It is responsible for providing essential services like water supply, sanitation, roads, and public health.
 
 
 
• **Municipal Corporation:**
 
 
• Municipal Corporations govern larger urban areas or metropolitan cities with populations exceeding 1 million.
 
• The Mayor is the political head of a Municipal Corporation, while the Municipal Commissioner serves as the administrative head.
 
• Examples of Municipal Corporations include the Delhi Municipal Corporation, Mumbai Municipal Corporation, etc.
 
 
 
• **Chief Municipal Officer:**
 
 
• The Chief Municipal Officer is the administrative head of a municipality.
 
• They are responsible for implementing the council's decisions and managing day-to-day administrative functions.
 
• This officer is usually appointed by the state government.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Chairman and Mayor:**
 
 
• The Chairman is the political head of a Municipal Council, while the Mayor is the political head of a Municipal Corporation.
 
• The Chairman represents smaller towns, whereas the Mayor represents larger cities.

questions.question: Besides resolving disputes, what power do the Nyaya Panchayats have in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Imposing fines on offenders**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Nyaya Panchayats** are judicial bodies established in rural areas of India to resolve local disputes and maintain harmony.
 
• They have the authority to **impose fines on offenders** as a corrective and punitive measure in civil and minor criminal cases.
 
• These fines act as a deterrent while ensuring justice is served without escalating disputes to higher courts.
 
• The jurisdiction of Nyaya Panchayats is generally limited to cases of minor disputes, including petty thefts, minor assaults, and simple civil disagreements.
 
• They play a crucial role in delivering **speedy and cost-effective justice** in rural India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nyaya Panchayat:**

 
 
• It is a village-level judicial system established under the **Gram Panchayat Act** in various states of India.
 
• It is a decentralized system aimed at reducing the burden on regular courts and improving access to justice in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Jurisdiction:**
 
 
• Nyaya Panchayats handle cases involving disputes related to property, breach of contract, and family matters.
 
• They have no jurisdiction over cases involving serious crimes or disputes requiring extensive legal expertise.
 
 
 
• **Limitations:**
 
 
• They do not have the authority to imprison offenders but can impose fines or other penalties within their prescribed limits.
 
• They function under the supervision of higher judicial authorities to ensure fairness and legality.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• Nyaya Panchayats promote localized and participatory governance by involving community members in dispute resolution.
 
• They play a vital role in reducing litigation costs and ensuring justice is accessible to rural populations.

questions.question: Which Fundamental Right was subjected to additional restrictions by the First Amendment Act of 1951?

options.text: Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The First Amendment Act of 1951 brought additional restrictions to the **Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression** under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.
 
• It introduced provisions allowing the state to impose "reasonable restrictions" on this right in the interests of **public order, security, decency, morality, sovereignty, and integrity of India.**
 
• The amendment was enacted to address issues arising from judicial interpretations that had invalidated several laws restricting speech and expression.
 
• The Act also added Article 19(2), which explicitly states the grounds on which the government can limit the right to freedom of speech and expression.
 
• This amendment was a response to decisions like the Romesh Thapar vs State of Madras case, where the Supreme Court struck down laws restricting press freedom.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights in India:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and are considered essential for individual freedom and democracy.
 
• They include rights such as equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, and constitutional remedies.
 
• These rights are enforceable by the judiciary and can be challenged in a court of law.
 
 
 
• **Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens, including the right to freedom of speech and expression.
 
• These freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions for maintaining public order, morality, and sovereignty.
 
 
 
• **Romesh Thapar vs State of Madras (1950):**
 
 
• This landmark case challenged restrictions imposed on the press under public order laws.
 
• The Supreme Court invalidated these laws, prompting the government to introduce the First Amendment Act.
 
 
 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:**
 
 
• The First Amendment introduced the concept of "reasonable restrictions" to ensure a balance between individual freedom and societal interests.
 
• Grounds for restriction include security, sovereignty, morality, and public order.

questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes the Indian President's role in foreign affairs?

options.text: The President delegates all foreign affairs responsibilities to the Prime Minister.
The President appoints ambassadors and conducts diplomatic work in his/her name.
The President only receives foreign ambassadors but does not appoint them
The President is solely responsible for negotiating international treaties without any advisory input.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The President appoints ambassadors and conducts diplomatic work in his/her name.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian President, as the head of state, exercises certain powers related to foreign affairs, including appointing ambassadors and conducting diplomatic actions in their name.
 
• All international treaties and agreements are signed in the name of the President, but they require ratification by Parliament to become binding.
 
• The President formally represents India in international forums and receives foreign ambassadors and dignitaries.
 
• While the President's role is largely ceremonial in foreign affairs, the Prime Minister and the Ministry of External Affairs handle the substantive and decision-making aspects.
 
• Constitutionally, the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers, led by the Prime Minister, in matters related to foreign policy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ambassadors:**

 
 
• Ambassadors are official representatives of a nation in foreign countries.
 
• They are appointed by the President of India based on recommendations from the Ministry of External Affairs.
 
• Ambassadors play key roles in promoting diplomatic relations, trade, and cultural exchanges.
 
 
 
• **International Treaties:**
 
 
• International treaties signed by the President must be approved by Parliament under Article 253 of the Constitution.
 
• Treaties cover a wide range of subjects, including trade, defense, and environmental agreements.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Prime Minister:**
 
 
• The Prime Minister leads foreign policy decision-making in consultation with the Cabinet.
 
• While the President represents India ceremonially, the Prime Minister negotiates and shapes international relations.
 
 
 
• **Ministry of External Affairs:**
 
 
• This ministry is responsible for India's foreign relations, trade agreements, and diplomatic missions.
 
• It coordinates closely with the President and Prime Minister to implement India's foreign policy.

questions.question: The President's power to seek the Supreme Court's opinion on questions of law comes under ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 143**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 143 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on questions of law or fact that are of public importance.
 
• The advice provided by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is not binding on the President; it is advisory in nature.
 
• This provision is often referred to as the "Advisory Jurisdiction" of the Supreme Court.
 
• Article 143 is invoked to resolve complex legal or constitutional matters that require judicial interpretation.
 
• The President can exercise this power either on his own discretion or based on advice from the Council of Ministers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Advisory Jurisdiction:**

 
 
• It is a unique feature of the Indian judiciary under Article 143, allowing the Supreme Court to provide opinions on matters referred by the President.
 
• Examples include cases related to the Berubari Union and the Ayodhya dispute.
 
• The court's opinion is purely advisory and does not have the force of a judicial decision.
 
 
 
• **Other Relevant Articles:**
 
 
• Article 131: Deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in disputes between states or between the union and states.
 
• Article 136: Provides the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal against any judgment or order.
 
• Article 226: Empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and other matters.
 
 
 
• **Role of the President:**
 
 
• The President acts as the constitutional head of the country and exercises powers based on provisions like Article 143.
 
• The decision to seek advice under Article 143 is often made based on significant national or legal concerns.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Article 143:**
 
 
• Article 143 ensures clarity and resolution in intricate legal and constitutional matters.
 
• It strengthens the consultative mechanism between the executive and the judiciary.

questions.question: Which provision was introduced in the Constitution of India through the 74th Amendment Act?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Part IX-A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **74th Amendment Act** of the Indian Constitution, enacted in **1992**, specifically introduced **Part IX-A**, which deals with the governance of **urban local bodies**.
 
• This amendment provides a **constitutional status** to urban local self-governments such as **Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, and Nagar Panchayats**.
 
• It aims to ensure **decentralization** in urban governance and encourage **grassroots democracy** in urban areas.
 
• **Article 243-P to Article 243-ZG** were added to the Constitution under Part IX-A, detailing the **composition, powers, and responsibilities** of urban local bodies.
 
• It mandates the establishment of **Ward Committees** in municipalities with a population of over **3 lakh**, ensuring greater **citizen participation**.
 
• The amendment also outlines provisions for the **reservation of seats** for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women in urban local bodies.
 
• A **State Finance Commission** is to be constituted to recommend measures for the financial health of these bodies.
 
• The 74th Amendment is significant for promoting **good governance** and addressing the challenges of **urbanization** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Part X**__

 __
 
• **Part X** of the Constitution deals with the **Scheduled and Tribal Areas**.
 
• It includes provisions for the administration and governance of these areas to protect the interests of **Scheduled Tribes**.
 
• It covers **Articles 244 and 244A**.
 
 
 
• **Part IX**__
 __
 
• **Part IX** of the Constitution deals with **Panchayati Raj Institutions** and was added through the **73rd Amendment Act, 1992**.
 
• It focuses on **rural local governance** and includes **Articles 243 to 243-O**.
 
 
 
• **Part XI**__
 
 
• **Part XI** of the Constitution deals with the **relations between the Union and the States**.
 
• It includes provisions related to **legislative and administrative relations**, covered under **Articles 245 to 263**.

questions.question: Who administers the oath of office and secrecy to the Union Ministers under Article 75(4) of the Constitution of India?

__
 
• Under **Article 75(4) of the Constitution of India**, the oath of office and secrecy is administered to the Union Ministers by the **President of India.**
 
• The oath is taken in accordance with the provisions of the **Third Schedule** of the Constitution.
 
• The President ensures that the Union Ministers pledge to uphold the **Constitution of India**, maintain secrecy, and perform their duties faithfully.
 
• The President is the head of the state and serves as the **constitutional authority** responsible for appointing Union Ministers as per the advice of the **Prime Minister.**
 
• This process reflects the principle of maintaining the integrity and solemnity of the **parliamentary democracy** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chief Justice of India**__

 __
 
• The **Chief Justice of India (CJI)** primarily heads the judiciary and does not administer the oath of office and secrecy to Union Ministers.
 
• The Chief Justice is responsible for interpreting the Constitution and overseeing the functioning of the **Supreme Court of India.**
 
• However, the CJI administers the oath to the **President of India and Governors** in specific circumstances.
 
 
 
• **Prime Minister**__
 __
 
• The **Prime Minister** acts as the head of the government and advises the President on the appointment of Union Ministers.
 
• While the Prime Minister plays a significant role in governance, he/she does not administer the oath to Union Ministers.
 
 
 
• **Vice President**__
 
 
• The **Vice President of India** is primarily responsible for officiating in the absence of the President and serves as the Chairman of the **Rajya Sabha.**

questions.question: The doctrine of judicial review originated in which country?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**United States of America**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The doctrine of **judicial review** originated in the **United States of America**.
 
• The concept was established through the landmark case of **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**, which was presided over by Chief Justice **John Marshall**.
 
• This case established the principle that the **Supreme Court of the United States** has the authority to review and invalidate laws and actions of the executive and legislative branches if they conflict with the **U.S. Constitution**.
 
• Judicial review is considered a fundamental aspect of the **separation of powers** and ensures that no branch of government exceeds its constitutional limits.
 
• The doctrine serves as a mechanism to protect the rights of individuals and maintain the supremacy of the **Constitution** in the governance of the country.
 
• In the United States, judicial review plays a critical role in maintaining the principle of **checks and balances** among the three branches of government: the legislative, executive, and judiciary.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **United Kingdom**__

 __
 
• The United Kingdom follows the principle of **parliamentary sovereignty**, meaning Parliament is the supreme legal authority.
 
• Unlike the United States, the concept of judicial review is limited in the UK. Courts cannot overrule legislation passed by Parliament but can review whether public authorities act within their legal powers.
 
 
 
• **India**__
 __
 
• India adopted the concept of **judicial review** from the United States, and it is enshrined in the Indian Constitution.
 
• Articles **13, 32, and 136** of the Indian Constitution empower courts to review the constitutionality of laws and executive actions.
 
 
 
• **France**__
 
 
• France follows the **civil law system**, and judicial review as in the U.S. does not exist.
 
• The **Constitutional Council** of France examines the constitutionality of laws but only before they are enacted, not after.

questions.question: Which union territory was added to India by the Fourteenth Amendment Act, 1962?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Puducherry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Fourteenth Amendment Act of **1962** enabled the integration of the Union Territory of **Puducherry** (formerly known as Pondicherry) into India.
 
• **Puducherry** was a former French colony, and its integration into India was formalized through a **treaty between India and France** signed in **1956**.
 
• The treaty was ratified by the French Parliament, and **Puducherry officially became part of India** on **16th August 1962**.
 
• The Union Territory of Puducherry includes four regions: **Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe,** and **Yanam**, which are geographically separated but collectively administered.
 
• Puducherry’s inclusion in India was a significant step towards consolidating the country’s territorial integrity post-independence.
 
• The region is known for its unique **French heritage, architecture, and culture**, which continue to influence its identity.
 
• Puducherry is governed under the provisions of **Article 239** of the Indian Constitution, which deals with the administration of Union Territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Goa**__

 __
 
• **Goa** was annexed by India from Portuguese control in **1961** through a military operation called **Operation Vijay**.
 
• It became a Union Territory initially but achieved statehood on **30th May 1987**.
 
 
 
• **Daman and Diu**__
 __
 
• **Daman and Diu** were also liberated from Portuguese control in **1961**, along with Goa.
 
• It remained a Union Territory until it was merged with Dadra and Nagar Haveli to form a new Union Territory in **2020**.
 
 
 
• **Lakshadweep**__
 
 
• **Lakshadweep** is a group of islands in the Arabian Sea, which became a Union Territory of India in **1956**.
 
• The islands are known for their **biodiversity, coral reefs, and tourism potential**.

questions.question: What happens if a no‑confidence motion is passed in the Indian Lok Sabha against the union government?

options.text: The Prime Minister is given a chance to reorganise the Cabinet.
The entire Council of Ministers must resign.

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The entire Council of Ministers must resign.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **No-Confidence Motion** is a parliamentary motion moved against the **Union Government**, indicating that the ruling government no longer holds the confidence of the majority of members in the **Lok Sabha**, as per **Article 75(3)** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• If the motion is passed, it leads to a loss of majority for the ruling government in the Lok Sabha, thereby mandating the resignation of the **entire Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister.**
 
• The **Prime Minister** and the Council of Ministers collectively hold office during the pleasure of the President, but this is contingent upon the government maintaining the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
 
• It is a crucial legislative mechanism to ensure the accountability of the government to the elected representatives of the people.
 
• Once the Council of Ministers resigns, the President may invite the leader of another party or coalition that can prove majority support to form the new government, or may call for fresh **general elections.**
 
• The process of a No-Confidence Motion ensures the stability and democratic functioning of India's parliamentary system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Prime Minister is given a chance to reorganise the Cabinet.**__

 __
 
• This option is incorrect because a No-Confidence Motion does not provide the Prime Minister with an opportunity to reorganize the Cabinet. Instead, the motion directly challenges the authority and legitimacy of the entire government.
 
• The motion signifies loss of majority support, making it mandatory for the entire Council of Ministers to resign.
 
 
 
• **Only the dissenting ministers resign.**__
 __
 
• In the parliamentary system, the Council of Ministers functions as a collective entity. Hence, resignation due to a No-Confidence Motion applies to the **entire Council of Ministers**, not just dissenting members.
 
• Individual resignations do not address the fundamental issue of lack of majority support in the Lok Sabha.
 
 
 
• **A re-election is triggered.**__
 
 
• While a No-Confidence Motion may eventually lead to fresh elections, it is not an automatic outcome of the motion being passed.
 
• The President can invite another party or coalition with a proven majority in the Lok Sabha to form the government before considering general elections.

questions.question:
For which of the given bills can the President of India summon a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament?

1. Ordinary Bill

2. Money Bill

3. Constitutional Amendment Bill
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**1 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **President of India** can summon a **joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament** under **Article 108** of the Constitution.
 
• This is applicable in cases of a legislative deadlock on an **Ordinary Bill**, where both Houses fail to agree on its passage.
 
• A joint sitting is presided over by the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha**, or in their absence, the Deputy Speaker.
 
• Joint sittings are convened to resolve disputes between the **Lok Sabha** and **Rajya Sabha** concerning an Ordinary Bill.
 
• The **Money Bill** and **Constitutional Amendment Bill** are excluded from this provision as they have distinct procedural requirements and do not fall under legislative deadlock scenarios.
 
• The joint sitting mechanism reflects the principle of resolving conflicts and ensuring the smooth functioning of the legislative process in a parliamentary democracy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Money Bill**__

 __
 
• A **Money Bill** is specifically defined under **Article 110** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It primarily deals with matters related to the **imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of taxes**, borrowing of money, expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, etc.
 
• The **Lok Sabha** has exclusive power to approve a Money Bill, while the **Rajya Sabha** can only recommend changes within a limited timeframe.
 
• No provision for a joint sitting exists for Money Bills, as the Lok Sabha holds greater authority in financial matters.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Amendment Bill**__
 
 
• A **Constitutional Amendment Bill** is governed under **Article 368** of the Constitution.
 
• Such bills are passed with a special majority in both Houses of Parliament, and there is no provision for a joint sitting to resolve differences.
 
• These bills often require ratification by at least half of the **State Legislatures** for amendments impacting the federal structure.
 
• The procedural requirements for Constitutional Amendment Bills are distinct from Ordinary Bills and Money Bills.

questions.question: Which two policy areas are explicitly managed by the Union Cabinet in India as part of its coordinating functions?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Foreign Relations and Defence**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Union Cabinet** in India explicitly manages **Foreign Relations** and **Defence** as part of its coordinating functions.
 
• Under **Article 73** of the Indian Constitution, the Union Government has exclusive powers to legislate on matters relating to **foreign affairs** and **defence.**
 
• **Foreign Relations** involve managing India’s diplomatic ties, treaties, trade agreements, and coordination with international organizations such as the **United Nations**.
 
• **Defence** encompasses the responsibility of ensuring national security, managing the armed forces (Army, Navy, and Air Force), and overseeing strategic operations.
 
• The Union Cabinet handles critical decisions such as signing international treaties, defense procurement, and deploying forces during crises.
 
• These areas are fundamental to maintaining the sovereignty, security, and global standing of India, which is why they are explicitly managed by the central government.
 
• The Ministry of **External Affairs** and the Ministry of **Defence** work in coordination with the Union Cabinet to implement policies in these domains.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Agriculture and Labour**__

 __
 
• **Agriculture** falls under the **State List** as per the Constitution of India, meaning that state governments primarily manage policies related to agriculture.
 
• **Labour** is included in the **Concurrent List**, which allows both the Union and State Governments to legislate on issues such as employment, wages, and industrial disputes.
 
• The Union Cabinet does intervene in labour matters for national-level policies, but these are not exclusively managed by the Union Cabinet.
 
 
 
• **Tourism and Sports**__
 __
 
• **Tourism** is primarily managed by the states, though the Union Government promotes national-level tourism campaigns and policies like **Incredible India**.
 
• **Sports** policies and development programs are largely coordinated by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, but these do not fall under the exclusive domain of the Union Cabinet.
 
 
 
• **Education and Health**__
 
 
• **Education** is part of the **Concurrent List**, and both Union and State Governments can legislate on matters related to schools, universities, and other educational institutions.
 
• **Health** is also in the **State List**, meaning state governments have primary responsibility for healthcare policies, though the Union Government coordinates national health schemes like **Ayushman Bharat**.

questions.question: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court of India rule that the Council of Ministers DOES NOT cease to hold office even after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?

options.text: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala, 1973
SR Bommai vs. Union of India, 1994

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**UNR Rao vs. Indira Gandhi, 1971**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The case of **UNR Rao vs. Indira Gandhi, 1971**, is a landmark judgment by the **Supreme Court of India**.
 
• In this case, the court ruled that the **Council of Ministers** does not cease to hold office even after the **dissolution of the Lok Sabha**.
 
• This judgment clarified that the Council of Ministers continues to function and assist the **President of India** in discharging their duties.
 
• The decision was based on the interpretation of **Article 74 of the Indian Constitution**, which provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President.
 
• This case established that the executive authority of the government does not come to a standstill with the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, ensuring continuity in governance.
 
• It highlights the importance of the principle of **collective responsibility** of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha, as enshrined in the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala, 1973**__

 __
 
• This case is famous for the **Basic Structure Doctrine**, which limits the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution.
 
• The court ruled that while Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, it cannot alter its **basic structure**.
 
• This case is considered a cornerstone in the history of **Indian constitutional law**.
 
 
 
• **Golaknath vs. State of Punjab, 1967**__
 __
 
• This case ruled that **Fundamental Rights** cannot be amended by Parliament.
 
• It declared that the Constitution's **Fundamental Rights** were sacrosanct and inviolable.
 
• However, this decision was later overturned by the Kesavananda Bharati case.
 
 
 
• **SR Bommai vs. Union of India, 1994**__
 
 
• This case is a landmark judgment in the context of the **President's Rule** under Article 356 of the Constitution.
 
• The court laid down the principles of judicial review of the imposition of **President's Rule**.
 
• It emphasized that the **secular character of the Constitution** is part of its basic structure.

questions.question: In some cases, the Prime Minister of India assigns an independent charge of a portfolio to a Minister of State. This implies that the Minister of State:

options.text: loses the title of Minister of State
serves jointly with a Cabinet Minister to share and perform responsibilities of the assigned portfolio
functions as if in Cabinet rank with full independent responsibility for that portfolio

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**functions as if in Cabinet rank with full independent responsibility for that portfolio**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An independent charge of a portfolio to a Minister of State implies that the Minister is entrusted with full responsibility of that portfolio without supervision from a Cabinet Minister.
 
• The Minister of State with independent charge is treated as equivalent to Cabinet rank in terms of responsibility for the specific portfolio.
 
• This arrangement is made when the Prime Minister decides that the portfolio does not require oversight by a Cabinet Minister.
 
• Such Ministers have the authority to make decisions and represent their ministries in Parliament, similar to a Cabinet Minister.
 
• While holding independent charge, the Minister of State reports directly to the Prime Minister.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Minister of State:**

 
 
• A Minister of State (MoS) is a junior minister in the Indian government who assists a Cabinet Minister in specific areas of their portfolio.
 
• They typically work under the supervision of a Cabinet Minister unless given independent charge.
 
 
 
• **Independent Charge:**
 
 
• When a Minister of State is given independent charge, they function autonomously for that portfolio without reporting to a Cabinet Minister.
 
• This arrangement is often used to optimize government functioning and delegate authority efficiently.
 
 
 
• **Cabinet Minister:**
 
 
• A Cabinet Minister is a senior member of the Council of Ministers responsible for major ministries such as Finance, Defence, or External Affairs.
 
• Cabinet Ministers hold the highest rank in the government after the Prime Minister.
 
 
 
• **Portfolio Allocation:**
 
 
• Portfolio allocation is the process by which the Prime Minister assigns specific ministries or departments to members of the Council of Ministers.
 
• The allocation depends on factors such as expertise, political considerations, and administrative requirements.

questions.question: The Recorder’s Court was later replaced by the ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Supreme Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Recorder's Court in India was replaced by the **Supreme Court** under the provisions of the Regulating Act of 1773.
 
• The Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William (Calcutta) was established in **1774** as the first Supreme Court in British India.
 
• The establishment of the Supreme Court aimed to introduce a unified judicial system in British-controlled territories.
 
• The Supreme Court had original, appellate, and admiralty jurisdiction and was intended to administer justice based on English law.
 
• The court replaced the Recorder's Court, which was earlier functioning in some British settlements in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Recorder's Court**

 
 
• The Recorder's Court was a type of court established by the British in colonial territories to handle legal matters.
 
• It was primarily tasked with adjudicating civil and criminal cases in British-controlled areas.
 
• The Recorder's Court was presided over by a judge known as the "Recorder."
 
 
 
• **Regulating Act of 1773**
 
 
• The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first attempt by the British government to regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India.
 
• It established the Supreme Court at Calcutta and marked the beginning of a centralized judicial system in India.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William**
 
 
• It was the first Supreme Court in India and was established in Calcutta in 1774.
 
• The court had jurisdiction over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
 
• It consisted of a Chief Justice and three other judges.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Evolution in British India**
 
 
• The judicial system evolved over time, with the creation of High Courts in 1862 and the abolition of the Supreme Court under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861.
 
• These High Courts eventually became the foundation of the Indian judicial system.

questions.question: Which court in the subordinate judiciary has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in civil cases?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Judge of District Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **District Court** serves as the principal court of original jurisdiction in civil matters in the subordinate judiciary system in India.
 
• The District Court is presided over by the **District Judge**, who has the authority to hear civil cases with **unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction** unless restricted by specific legislative provisions.
 
• These courts handle a wide range of civil disputes, including property disputes, matrimonial cases, and contractual disagreements, among others.
 
• District Courts are established by state governments in India for every district or group of districts, as per the **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908**.
 
• The decisions of the District Court can be appealed to the **High Court** of the respective state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pecuniary Jurisdiction:**

 
 
• Pecuniary jurisdiction refers to the monetary value of cases that a particular court is authorized to hear and adjudicate.
 
• In India, lower courts like the Court of Munsiff typically have limited pecuniary jurisdiction, while District Courts have no upper monetary limit unless restricted by state laws.
 
 
 
• **Hierarchy of Civil Courts:**
 
 
• The hierarchy of civil courts in India includes the Court of Munsiff, Civil Judge (Junior Division), Civil Judge (Senior Division), and District Courts.
 
• Above the subordinate courts, civil matters can be escalated to the High Courts and, in some cases, the Supreme Court of India.
 
 
 
• **Small Causes Court:**
 
 
• Small Causes Courts deal with cases related to small monetary disputes, typically with a value below a certain threshold, which varies by state.
 
• They lack jurisdiction over cases involving property disputes or other significant civil matters.
 
 
 
• **Nyaya Panchayat:**
 
 
• Nyaya Panchayats are grassroots-level judicial bodies in rural areas that handle minor civil and criminal cases.
 
• They focus on delivering speedy and cost-effective justice but have limited jurisdiction and authority.
 
 
 
• **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908:**
 
 
• This is the primary legislation governing the functioning and procedures of civil courts in India.
 
• It defines the jurisdiction, powers, and structure of courts, including the District Courts and subordinate courts.

questions.question: Who among the following first coined the term 'judicial activism'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arthur Schlesinger Jr.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

 
• Arthur Schlesinger Jr., a renowned American historian and social critic, first coined the term **'judicial activism'** in a 1947 article titled “The Supreme Court: 1947” published in Fortune magazine.
 
• The term was used to describe the behavior of judges who go beyond their traditional role of interpreting the law and actively shape policy decisions through their rulings.
 
• Schlesinger Jr. categorized Supreme Court justices of his time into "judic
